LLMs, Multimodal & Agentic AI

Studying systems that interpret language, images and sensor signals, and the emerging behaviors of interacting AI agents.

Research Description

Overview

We study LLMs, VLMs and multimodal models that interpret language, images and sensor information, alongside emerging agentic AI workflows. Key questions concern whether outputs remain grounded in input evidence, how modalities interact under attack and how privacy changes when people use AI assistants.

Published VLM robustness and consumer-assistant studies sit alongside emerging work on agent-to-agent interactions and multimodal screening prototypes. The goal is to characterize capabilities and failure modes with clear evaluation limits, rather than equating fluent responses with reliable decisions.

Research Thrusts

Grounded multimodal interpretation

Study how language, images and sensing signals contribute to model outputs, distinguishing evidence-grounded interpretation from fluent but unsupported responses.

Privacy and adversarial reliability

Evaluate LLM/VLM behavior in consumer tools and adversarial settings, including driving-scene understanding and writing-assistant privacy.

Emerging agent interactions

Explore agent-to-agent behavior and multimodal agent prototypes, with explicit attention to evaluation boundaries and edge–cloud constraints.

Research Goals

Evaluate multimodal capabilities and vulnerabilities, privacy in AI assistance, and agent interactions.

Intellectual Merit

Connect evidence across modalities and interaction settings, testing reliability instead of assuming that fluent output is correct.

Research Impact

The goal is a stronger basis for evaluating AI assistants and multimodal workflows before they are trusted in consequential settings. Exploratory agent and screening prototypes are not evidence of validated autonomous or clinical performance.

Current Projects & Emerging Directions

Existing research

Privacy in human–AI interaction

Text / audio→Consumer AI transformation→Privacy ↔ utility

Everyday writing and audio-editing tools may reveal sensitive attributes, but may also help transform content to reduce unwanted inference. The same consumer interface can therefore act as both a privacy risk and a possible defense.

Research objectives

Measure how transformations affect sensitive-attribute inference while preserving the usefulness and meaning of the original content.

Approach & Intellectual Merit

Published writing-assistant and audio-editing studies motivate controlled comparisons across original and transformed inputs. Privacy protection, task utility and model-specific behavior must be assessed together; fluent rewrites alone do not demonstrate protection.

Selected publications

No Innocence in Styling: Discovery of Privacy Protection Capabilities and Security Risks in Consumer Generative AI Writing Assistants ↗

Relevance & Applications

Relevant settings include consumer platforms, communication tools and device-integrated assistants using LLMs. Results support informed evaluation of privacy tradeoffs, not universal guarantees across people, models or platforms.

Impact

The published work examines both privacy-protection capabilities and security risks. It may help researchers and users assess tradeoffs, but does not establish universal privacy guarantees or measured adoption outcomes.

Existing research

Language models for cyber-physical systems

Physical observations→Language-assisted interpretation→Human oversight

Language models can connect sensor observations with human-readable descriptions and higher-level decisions. Physical environments also impose constraints that text-only benchmarks may miss, including timing, incomplete measurements and consequences of erroneous outputs.

Research objectives

Explore useful language-assisted sensing and interpretation while preserving privacy, reliability and resource awareness.

Approach & Intellectual Merit

Published architectures and fall-detection studies provide foundations, alongside wearable-data integrity research. The evaluation agenda connects sensor evidence to model output and considers uncertainty and human oversight rather than assuming autonomous control is safe.

Selected publications

Adaptive and Robust Data Poisoning Detection and Sanitization in Wearable IoT Systems using Large Language Models ↗

Relevance & Applications

Applications include smart environments, wearable assistance and healthcare-oriented research prototypes. Each setting requires separate testing of detection errors, response behavior and user impact.

Impact

The aim is to connect useful language-model capabilities with the privacy, security, and resource requirements of physical environments. The linked wearable-data study is supporting research, not evidence of clinical deployment or validated autonomous control.

Published foundations and emerging preprints

Multimodal robustness and agent interactions

Multimodal evidence→Models & agent interactions→Robustness assessment

Vision–language models combine complementary evidence but can be vulnerable when an input is perturbed or modalities disagree. Interacting agents add another layer: one system’s outputs can become another system’s context or decision input.

Research objectives

Characterize robustness across modalities and investigate behavior across agent-to-agent interactions.

Approach & Intellectual Merit

Published VLM robustness studies and emerging agent-interaction preprints form distinct evidence streams. The evaluation agenda connects input evidence, model response and interaction outcomes while keeping prototype results separate from deployment claims.

Relevance & Applications

Relevant research settings include driving scenes, consumer AI and the VetClaw veterinary screening prototype. These studies do not establish validated autonomous driving, clinical screening performance or general-purpose agent reliability.

Impact

Evidence for evaluating vulnerabilities and prototype behavior, not validated autonomous driving or clinical performance.
